title: Indian Cuisine Gets Its Own Oscars: Inside the Inaugural Global Indian Restaurant Awards in London
excerpt: From Sanjeev Kapoor to the Cinnamon Club, the first-ever international edition of India's most prestigious restaurant awards crowned the chefs and brands redefining Indian food worldwide.
body:
The Royal Lancaster Hotel in London played host to a historic gathering on May 28 when the Indian Restaurant Congress & Awards held its first-ever international edition, bringing together 250 restaurateurs, Michelin-starred chefs, and hospitality innovators from across the globe.

## A National Platform Goes Global

For 14 years, the Indian Restaurant Awards has been the gold standard for India's food and beverage industry, documenting the evolution of Indian dining and connecting thousands of restaurateurs with investors and strategic insights. The 2026 Global Edition marks a deliberate pivot from a national powerhouse to a global authority — and the choice of London, home to what is arguably the world's most competitive Indian restaurant scene, was no accident.

The event's theme, "The Global Rise of Indian Food Brands," set the tone for a summit that explored cross-border investment, the chef-to-entrepreneur pipeline, and how Indian dining concepts are scaling internationally. A panel titled "Beyond the Kitchen" featured two-time Michelin-starred chef Atul Kochhar alongside Vivek Singh of the Cinnamon Collection and Cyrus Todiwala OBE of Café Spice Namasté, all of whom have built restaurant empires from London.

## The Winners

The evening culminated in an awards ceremony that read like a who's who of global Indian gastronomy. Sanjeev Kapoor — the chef whose television show *Khana Khazana* shaped how an entire generation of Indians learned to cook — was named Global Indian Chef of the Year. Atul Kochhar, who in 2001 became the first Indian chef to receive a Michelin star, took home the Culinary Excellence Award.

The Cinnamon Club, the iconic Westminster restaurant that helped pioneer the fine-dining Indian restaurant concept in London over two decades ago, won Global Indian Restaurant of the Year. Jamavar, the Leela Group's luxury brand with locations in London, Doha, and Mumbai, was named Best Indian Restaurant Brand. The Tresind group, which has expanded from Dubai to Mumbai and beyond, claimed Restaurant Group of the Year.

Other notable winners included Kahani for Best Fine Dining, Benares for Best Chef-Led Restaurant, Colonel Saab for Best Indian Restaurant in the United Kingdom, and Dastaan for Best Indian Neighbourhood Restaurant.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For the estimated 32 million Indians living abroad, the London awards represent something beyond culinary recognition. They are a validation of what diaspora food lovers have long known — that Indian cuisine is not a niche category but a global force.

The timing is significant. Indian restaurant brands are expanding into the US, Middle East, and Southeast Asia at an unprecedented pace. In the United States alone, concepts like Dishoom (valued at nearly $400 million after a private-equity deal), Gymkhana, and Farzi Café are either already open or preparing to launch. Sanjeev Kapoor's Yellow Chilli is set to open in Santa Clara, California, next summer.

"This inaugural international summit brings together top restaurateurs, Michelin-starred chefs, and hospitality innovators to explore the future of dining," the organizers said, "bridging Indian heritage with global innovation."

## What's Next

The main Indian Restaurant Congress will return to New Delhi in December 2026 for its 15th edition at Bharat Mandapam, with over 2,000 delegates and 150 award categories expected. But the London edition has established a clear precedent: Indian cuisine's conversation is no longer contained within India's borders. For NRIs who have spent years explaining the difference between butter chicken and tikka masala to their neighbors, that shift matters more than any award.
author: Diaspora Desk
